utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Above ground.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's enough. I think I have a clearer picture. Because the idea that I had got was completely different. So it's my fault definitely. Now it's clear.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could you just take the map again, 757.1, just very quickly and just indicate to us where the cemetery was located.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The Greda cemetery is here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So close --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This area here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So close to the Partisan cemetery.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry -- yes. Yes. That's correct. That's Susnjar, the Partisan cemetery, and this here is Greda. And between these two cemeteries, there's also the Serbian, the Catholic, and the Jewish cemeteries. So this entire area here is used for cemeteries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Yes, thank you very much. Can we --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I can just note in passing as I go through the next document in the bundle which has already been marked Exhibit 211 is simply -- it shows the Crisis Staff decision from the -- the regional Crisis Staff was forwarded to Sanski Most. Then could we look, please, next at document numbered Prosecutor's Exhibit 648, which can be found behind divider 21. It's a Crisis Staff decision of the 30th of May, 1992. It talks about the people accommodated in the sports hall. And then at the bottom -- and citizens who have not been affected by combat operations and not warned to leave the area should stay where they were or return. "Condemnation of looting, arson, and destruction of unprotected property." And finally 5: "The Red Cross and other humanitarian organisations, charities, and individuals shall provide assistance in taking care of refugees from our area and elsewhere." Apparently this was sent to the Sanski Most radio station. Were you aware of the Red Cross giving assistance at any stage around this period of time, the 30th of May -- end of May, beginning of June?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Bosniak and Croat citizens did not have any access to the Serbian Red Cross. They provided food for their own refugees, those who had allegedly come to Sanski Most from other areas. I know that for a fact because my mother still remembers those days. And the woman who worked in the Red Cross, our neighbour, she asked them to give her some cans and some bread and they refused to give her any, saying that this was not for them. And she still remembers it, and she refuses to even look at that woman who worked in the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Can we move then, please, to the next document, Prosecutor's Exhibit 649. Now, this is one I think you personally handed to Ms. Paczulla from the Office of the Prosecutor. It's a proclamation issued apparently by -- to the Crisis Staff by the Sanski Most SOS dissociating themselves from the repeated and in recent times increasingly frequent hostile propaganda reports about the behaviour of the SOS asking for protection, stating that, "All our actions we have taken so far were intended to protect citizen and their property, their rights and freedoms. These actions were undertaken in agreement with the legal authorities, the official bodies, and the command of the 6th Krajina Brigade." And ending up by saying that they've decided to leave, "Fight for the Serbian cause outside the area of Sanski Most in the territory of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. Only unity can save the Serbs." Now, I don't know. Did you ever hear this proclamation or announcement on the radio whilst you were in prison? You told us you heard quite a lot of radio broadcasts.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not hear this proclamation on the radio.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: But if I may say just very briefly, this is a proclamation made by the SOS addressed to the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. We -- I don't think I'd said that. Sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, Ms. Korner. Judge, be patient with me, please. In the English version that I have right in front of me here, I have indicated the following: That there is a stamp which says "Serbian defence forces." And then there is a note "SM-66/2 added by hand." Now, if you look at the document in your language, there is indeed a stamp. Next to it, there is "SOS Sanski Most." We are not concerned about that. To the left, there is indeed a note saying "SM-66/2." There is a stamp. Can you tell me what are the words that appear on that stamp and whether I am right in suggesting to you also that although in the English version I have "Serbian defence forces," there is also the words "SOS" appearing on that stamp in your language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The stamp reads: "Serbian defence forces Sanski Most." That's written around the stamp. And then on the inside, there is the abbreviation "SOS," and then there is also the 4-S emblem. And to the right, there is the signature of the person who actually signed this document on behalf of the SOS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What was that 4-S emblem supposed to be? What does it stand for? Whose emblem is that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is the Serbian emblem, the emblem of the SDS. But it was accepted also as the national emblem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And the "SOS" stands for "Serbian defence forces."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That is correct. That, I know. Yes, thank you, Ms. Korner. I am really concerned that some -- something like this is omitted from the English version, because it's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I think, Your Honour, we've already looked at this problem before. Each translator is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't think I have to concentrate to the extent that I have to check every single document once, twice, to make sure that the translation is perfect and that nothing important or not important -- I don't know. If it's a translation, there should be nothing, absolutely nothing omitted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, we can only say, as I think I've had a number of occasions before, our ability to carefully check each translation is very limited. We have to rely on the translators. And it's only when one comes to look at individual documents in this way that one sees -- one notices matters.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while that matter is on the floor, so to speak, if -- just for guidance, if we find a document that has been mistranslated --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please. And you have in the past already.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes. How would you like us to bring that to your attention.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Bring it to our attention in the -- in the -- in whichever way you prefer. But it is important.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because documents can be neutral, can be in favour of the Defence, or can be in favour of the Prosecution. We have a duty to make sure -- a responsibility to make sure that if there is a document which is translated -- and we will be looking at the English translation -- that we are not misled into looking at something and reading something which does not represent faithfully the original. I mean, that's -- so if there are any documents of the kind, Mr. Ackerman - and there have been, because you -- you have signalled some of them in the course of the proceedings - if there are any more, please let us know.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, we found one last night. It's a case of an incomplete translation, and we'll bring it to your attention tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please do. Please do. I know also that I am facing you, Ms. Korner, with this problem. I know that it is not -- it cannot be attributed to you or that you are in any way responsible for it. I mean, I know that -- you are not accountable for the translation efforts or mistakes of the translators.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But you must I'm sure agree that this is important. You know, I mean --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I fully agree. And I do accept responsibility, although I can't check it. But it is like everything here, when possible -- certainly Ms. Richterova who does read the language occasionally has picked up real errors in translation. But for the rest of us, it's just a matter of, you know, hoping that it's properly done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But as I say I'm grateful to Mr. Ackerman or his team or indeed Madam Fauveau could bring it to our attention, we will try and get it corrected straight away. And we have, of course, through witnesses also spotted errors.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Saying, for example -- again, I mean something which may be less important but which is nevertheless important. If you look at the Serb -- Serbian/Croat version, you will see that the last paragraph, first two lines, second line being incomplete, are underlined.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Now, on previous occasions, this was indicated -- for example, if you look at the previous document, 648, whatever is underlined in the Serbo-Croat document is underlined in the English version. In this particular document, 649, this is not the case. Why do I have to look and compare the two versions -- fortunately this is just one page. But it could -- we could be speaking of -- of a document which is 100 pages long. Why do I have to -- to make this exercise all the way to see whether -- whatever was underlined in the original has been underlined in the English version and so on and so forth. I mean, it's --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, Your Honour, I think all that has been said -- and maybe it's repetitive -- that we can -- witnesses when they're going through the documents draw things to our attention. Equally, if there's something important the Defence notice, no doubt they'll bring it to the attention, and we'll try and do the same. But translation is not a computer-style art. It is an art.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I know.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And I'm afraid it's a matter that perhaps Your Honour may wish to raise with the translation department.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I will, once I have a little bit more flesh on the bones, because I'm not going to raise the matter on -- with the translation department only because of one single document. Obviously. I mean, it's ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Can we just please, then, move to the next document, which is marked Prosecutor's Exhibit P218. It's the following divider. Dated the 30th of May, and it lists -- it's conclusions of the Crisis Staff -- lists the members and their various jobs. And here we can see that apart from the people that you've mentioned, Mr. Savanovic, who's come up quite a lot, was president of the club of deputies of the SDS assembly. And there we I see Branko Basara, the 6th Krajina Brigade commander. "Crisis Staff meetings must be held every day." And then this one, circled -- in the B/C/S version it's circled, so -- Your Honour should be happy that the translator there has done that. "A long-term solution is to be found for the problem of refugees from the Mahala area as well as the Muslims and Croats who are not loyal to the constitution and laws of the Serbian Republic of BH, which means that is all those who have not taken up arms and want to change their municipality are to be allowed to move away. Also make contact with the leadership of the Autonomous Region of Krajina regarding implementation of the idea on resettlement of the population." You told us that before you were imprisoned, numbers of Muslims and Croats had left the municipality. As far as people in the Mahala area -- because that's what it refers to -- were concerned, from your knowledge after the attack were they resettled by the -- the Crisis Staff or did they leave of their own accord? In other words, under their own steam.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The population of Mahala had been expelled from Mahala and indeed from Sanski Most. The first transport took place, I think, on the 3rd of June. Around seven or eight hundred people -- women, children, men -- of various ages. They first took them to Mrkonjic Grad, intending to kick them out to Jajce and Travnik. But since they failed to do so due to some events that were taking place there, they brought the transport back and then took them to Bosanska Krupa right away and let them go across the bridge.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I think you told us --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Towards Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. Okay. Could we move, please, to the next document. And effectively this is on the same theme -- Exhibit P650 -- and really I think relates to what we've seen in the earlier documents, that the "Serbian Territorial Defence shall prevent all persons from entering the Mahala area except for authorised organs who are involved in mopping up." Can I just ask you, the word has been translated as "mopping up." Could you tell us what the actual -- if you can -- what the word is - I'm sorry - and how you understand it. What's the actual word in B/C/S?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I will read it. "The Crisis Staff issues an order to the Serbian Territorial Defence tasking it -- tasking the Serbian Territorial Defence with blocking the entrance -- in other words, prohibiting -- to block, means to stop --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: -- People from entering the area of Mahala.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Except for -- I understand that. It's the word that I want to know about. What do you understand -- what is your understanding of the word in your own language which is translated to us as "mopping up"? What does that actually mean to you?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm really sorry. I don't understand the word "mopping up" as it was said in the original.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I quite agree with you that it was simple enough. But let me try and simplify it further. Please look at the last four words in that order. Could you read them in your own language.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [B/C/S spoken]

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What do they mean?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That means that the services that have been authorised or charged by the Crisis Staff are allowed to enter Mahala and clean it up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: For what purpose? Clean it up.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my mind, that would be the removal of the dead bodies and also the searching of the various buildings and also looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Previous translation continues] ... Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you very much, Your Honour. I'm grateful for all help.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we now move, please, then to Prosecutor's Exhibit P --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, I have to --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Interject in this. We have official interpreters, Your Honour, and the -- I'm sitting here next to someone who knows the language. The language used has nothing to do with removal of dead bodies and looting.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I know that. It definitely means cleaning up.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She tells me that the more accurate interpretation is "cleaning up."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Cleaning up. Yes. That's how I understood it. You are right, Mr. Ackerman. The rest is how the witness understands it. But ...

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I agreement Your Honour, it -- I absolutely agree that the literal translation is --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Is "cleaning it up."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Is "cleaning it up." Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, can we move -- I said I'd try and finish before the break -- to the next document, please, Exhibit -- Prosecutor's Exhibit 652. This, I think, is a document simply to note because you provided it directly yourself. It's another executive committee decision -- or minutes of a session. I'm sorry. So we can leave that, please. 653 -- the next document, Prosecutor's Exhibit 653. This is a military document of sorts, it looks like. Yes, because it's signed by Colonel Basara -- dated the 1st of June, 1992, containing some orders. Order 1: "All soldiers drinking, et cetera, should be discharged. All soldiers prone to committing genocide against people, unable to conduct an armed struggle, must be discharged. All soldiers prone to burning down and destroying buildings from which the enemy is not opening fire at the unit must be discharged," et cetera. And then this. 2: "In future B/D -- I'm not sure what that's supposed to mean -- anyhow, we must not repeat the mistakes we have made before in the treatment of prisoners. No one has the right to beat or abuse prisoners when they are brought in until questioning has been carried out. Any soldier who abuses prisoners must be discharged from the unit without delay." You remained in the prison at the police station until the 17th of June. This is dated the 1st of June. Was there a difference that you noted in any of your treatment, those of you who --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Let -- Madam Fauveau, let her finish the question first, and then I'll hear your objection. Ms. Korner, please.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Was there any difference, first of all, that you noted in the treatment you were receiving; and second, from people who were being brought into the prison by the army?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before you proceed to answer the question, Judge, let me hear Madam Fauveau's objection. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. FAUVEAU-IVANOVIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I don't see how in a police station the treatment of prisoners could have been different on the basis of a military order. On the other hand, what Mrs. Korner added about the persons who had been brought in by the military police, I doubt that the witness was able to see by whom the other prisoners had been brought in. And in addition, I doubt that the witness is in a position to know what happened before the prisoners were brought into the police station.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, do you -- do you want to comment on that objection before I decide it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I take the -- I take the objection as justified to the first part of question. I think that does -- on reflection, that's right. As far as the second part is concerned, he said there were people being brought into his cell all the time who had been arrested by the military police. I'm entitled to ask whether he noticed any signs --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well, I think first you ask him whether he is -- whether he can confirm to us that they were indeed arrested by the military police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: If his answer is yes, we'll proceed. If his answer is "I don't know, I can't confirm," then we'll see.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Very well.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Judge, you've heard that. Do you know whether prisoners who were brought in whilst you were at the police station were arrested by military police or soldiers?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was in prison in the police station, there was a total of 16 or 17 of us. We were arrested in the first three days. So that's the 25th, the 26th and the 27th -- and perhaps on the 28th too. This figure did not change.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We were not in a position to know what was happening.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I'm grateful.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: In that case, I've decide not to pursue it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So your question ends there, Ms. Korner.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It does. It does.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Could we move then, please, to the next document, Prosecutor's Exhibit 380, which is -- yes. Actually I'm not sure?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm conscious of the time. So I think I'll leave that. It deals with the actions in Kamicak and Vrhpolje. But I don't think there's much point in asking this witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Prosecutor's Exhibit, please -- I'm sorry. I've lost -- yes. I'm sorry. I've lost my -- that was 380 -- 658, which is after divider 33. Now, again we're back to the subject of graves. An order by the municipal civilian protection staff, dated the 2nd of June, 1992. "In order to clear the area of Vrhpolje and Hrustovo from the destruction of war, bodies should urgently be recovered, identified, and buried in the designated place, a marked burial site." Very simply, you described the exhumations. Were any of those marked burial sites?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This order is comical. All the graves in Vrhpolje and Hrustovo were concealed. No one knew where they were. There were no markings of any kind. We searched for these graves. We -- they were dug at night. We examined them. They were dug at night with heavy machines. And this was done by people from the Serbian side who were trusted.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. Thank you. Could we move then, please, very quickly to Prosecutor's Exhibit -- sorry. I've now lost it. Sorry -- yes, 661, please, which is behind divider number 37. A Crisis Staff decision dated the 4th of June, 1992 where the conclusion number 1 is that "Vrucinic, Rasula, and Anicic shall be in charge of resolving the issue of prisoners and their categorisation and deportation to Manjaca. First category: Politicians. Second category: Nationalist extremists. Third category: People unwelcome in Sanski Most municipality. In view of this, have a talk with Colonel Stevilovic [phoen] from the 1st Krajina Corps." You told us that the first transport from the prison to Manjaca was the 6th of June.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Perhaps on the 3rd of June too.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I see. It's alleged that the first category of persons to be taken to Manjaca was politicians. Did that equate with what happened? Were the first people who went from your prison politicians?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's difficult for me to say whether they were politicians. They were ordinary people. I was transported on the 17th of June. The SDA politicians, I think they stayed on till the last, in the Krings Hall and in the prison and in the Betonirka place. And it wasn't until August that they were transported. They were the last to be transported. If we are referring to the leadership of the SDA party, of HDZ party, and so on.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Thank you. All right. Can we then move, please, to Prosecutor's Exhibit P665, which is behind divider 41. A Crisis Staff conclusion of the 6th of June, ordering the public security station to evacuate 150 prisoners and take them to Manjaca. So I think that's just confirming really the date that was in that original decision. Prosecutor's Exhibit -- could you move on please, to, Prosecutor's Exhibit -- well, no. Don't move.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Just to note in passing, Your Honour, that's repeated again with the same date. It's the actual order, I think.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: So could we come, please, to document P667, behind divider 43. And this, I think, is a document that you yourself handed over to the representative of the Office of the Prosecutor. I think it goes along with some of the lists you produced yesterday. But can you just tell us where you found this list or where this list came from.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This list comes from the service of the interior, the public security station in Sanski Most. I took it from the documents in the file, which I spoke about yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. And then if we look at the next document as well, which is P668. I think we'll find it's the same list but with effectively what action has been taken in respect of some of these people. And the third -- the third one is a list of what's headed "The most radical extremists in the area of Sanski Most." And I think you've already told us quite a lot about these people. We note that number 50 is Mirzet Karabeg. 49 is Suad -- is that Sabic or Sahic?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sabic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. It's quite difficult if one looks at the original?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Under number 42, Hase Osmancevic.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They're ordinary citizens, respected citizens from Sanski Most and from the neighbourhoods, both of Muslim and Croatian nationality but mainly of Muslim nationality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And can we -- sorry. And can we take it that comes also from the files held at the public security station?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Ms. Korner, just in the second page of Exhibit P668, before this list of the most radical extremists. I notice under number 60, the witness's own name. If he can confirm that. And next to it, there is a note saying "renew talk," and something illegible, "meeting with policemen." And "meeting with policemen" seems to be one of the reasons for which he may have been arrested in the first place if you look at the notes against some of the other names, like "arms smuggling," "renew questioning."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: "Renew talk link with R. about brother, Colonel Metahalagic [phoen]," and so on and so forth. So perhaps witness can -- if he has some information to give us on this, he can perhaps tell us.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Perhaps you could look -- could you read to us if you can read it, because the translator couldn't, what's said against your name?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It says "renew talk." And there is a word here that I can't understand. And then it says "a meeting with policemen." I can read that. When I was in Manjaca camp, these criminal inspectors, Branko Sobot and Milan Dobrijevic, also called Mima, and a member of the state security from Prijedor who was responsible for Sanski Most, Jugoslav Rodic, they took me out to be questioned and I was questioned -- or rather, I was told that I had been at a meeting for the formation of the Muslim police.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I spoke to them on that occasion, and naturally I was afraid because I thought that in the course of that questioning I would be killed. That was the meeting when the policemen, Bosniaks and Croats, were expelled from the public security station. And after that, they held a meeting in the fire brigade hall in Sanski Most. That would be it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, anyhow, you're no doubt happy to note that you're not regarded as one of the most radical extremists. Yes. Can we move, please, to the next document in the list that I want you to look at, Prosecutor's Exhibit 673, which can be found behind divider 51?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. Just a minute. These people were not extremists.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The people included in this list that you have mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes, I -- you said that. I'm sorry. It was an inappropriate remark, Judge, and I apologise. Can I ask you to look now at 673, which is behind divider number 51. This is an official note in respect of an incident that I think you mentioned apparently. On the 11th of June, a convoy of -- from Sanski Most to Manjaca containing 51 persons with an escort, and then on the section of road from Kozice to Hazici the first vehicle broke down and when the convoy stopped on a blind corner the persons began to jump out. We tried to prevent this by firing shots into the air in order to frighten them and then continued on our way to Manjaca. When we arrived at the barracks in Manjaca and were handing the persons over, we found out that six were missing." And it list it is names of the six. Do you know anything about that incident from people you spoke to at Manjaca?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: When this group arrived in Manjaca -- rather, when I arrived in Manjaca, because this group had arrived before me and when I was transferred from the stables where I was being kept in isolation to barn number 1, I then found out from the people in that barn, from people who had been in that convoy, that two groups of our people, of our fellow citizens, had been returned from Manjaca in those lorries in which they had been brought there. One of them had even been killed in Manjaca itself, because these people had been beaten in Manjaca and were then put back in the lorry. That was on the 6th of June and on the 12th of June -- or perhaps on the 11th of June. I think it was on the 12th.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I'm sorry. Could I stop for a moment. I just want to make sure we're on the same wavelength. This is apparently reporting that on the 11th of June, six people escaped from a transport to Manjaca. Do you know whether or not that is an accurate reflection of what happened? That's all I'm asking. If you don't -- if you don't know about this particular incident, say so.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this is an official note made by Milorad Krunic, an official, on the 11th of June, 1992. I think he is referring to an event that took place on the 6th of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. I think that perhaps we better leave -- leave it, because it may be that -- but are you -- I'm sorry. Can I ask -- are you aware, were you ever told by anyone after you mixed with your fellow prisoners in Manjaca that there had been six people who had managed to escape from a transport?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never. I was never told that people had escaped from a transport. This is pure fabrication. Those people would have appeared somewhere by now and we would have found out that they were either alive or dead.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you know any of these people?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If they had escaped from a transport. That's not correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: But --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Because Danilusko's letter provides an answer to this, provides an answer to your question.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Of the -- I'm sorry. Are you --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The letter I spoke about a few days ago here.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. Are you saying these are the people that were killed by Kajtez?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, that's what I'm saying. They were killed by the people who escorted them, who took them to Manjaca and who returned them from Manjaca. They killed them on the way from Manjaca to Sanski Most. And to this very day, we don't know where their grave is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, that's my --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Some Serbs told us about a location which we have been examining.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, it's my fault. I should have -- I forgot to tie up the names that -- with this.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And I think that's the only other document in this volume that I want you to look at?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm sorry. I generally thought I could finish, but with the discussion -- I don't have that many documents in volume 2, except that it may be -- if Your Honour wants to take a break. I think I will now take the rest of the session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's okay. Sorry about that --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sorry about that, Mr. Ackerman, and Madam Fauveau, because presumably you were gearing up to start your cross-examination just after the break. I apologise to you. It's something on which we have no control. And -- yeah. We'll continue in 30 minutes' time. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If the witness could be given volume 2 of the Sanski Most documents.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Could we start with the document, please, P680, which is immediately -- the first document in the bundle.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And of course, Ms. Korner, it's the last document in mine.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I had hoped that Your Honours' secretary had been put back to work and to redo it last night.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Oh, I asked her, actually. I mean, her idea was that eventually -- she has filed -- or she is filing all the exhibits of the Prosecution and of the Defence sequentially, as I had instructed her to in the beginning, only that then she has to dig up some of them as we proceed from one witness to another. And she said she finds it easier than to put them back where they belong that way rather than having them filed. And maybe she's -- she's not off the mark, because I can quite understand that makes her life easier, at least, and also mine to an extent.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But the sequentially -- it doesn't help. Because Your Honour -- what happened -- the reason why it doesn't work entirely is one, when Dr. Donia was here, they were all given exhibit numbers. But these exhibits in one -- onwards. But these exhibits then reappear in the various binders.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. This is it. So then she knows where to find them because they are exhibited in sequence.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And then she -- once for example, we're finished with this witness and we're talking of Exhibits 82, 160, which do not really belong to the Sanski Most municipality but they come from the Banja Luka one. So they go back where they belong. But anyway, let's proceed with the questioning.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: This is really just a report upon -- from the SJB to the CSB about the events that I think we've already dealt with, describing -- and I think I needn't ask you about this, because it describes the action of peaceful disarming and surrendering of weapons carried out in the period between the 10th and 25th of May. And during this period, "The Muslim and Croatian population handed over only hunting weapons and other legally owned weapons but illegally obtained military weapons were not surrendered and were concealed." And it perhaps answers the question as to whether Muslims and Croats were allowed to keep legally registered weapons. And then it describes the various actions from the point of view of the SJB against Mahala and the other places. It does describe -- can I just ask you this: From your investigations, it states that in the Muslim villages of Vrhpolje and Hrustovo, there was a Muslim force of 800 men broken up and military defeated while the houses were destroyed and burnt down. Army units casualties amounted to 12 men killed and eight wounded. Of the number of killed and wounded on the other side is unknown. Now, just very simply, from your investigations into these attacks on Vrhpolje and Hrustovo, would you agree with a figure of 800 men -- the Muslim force of 800 men?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have already mentioned -- I think, in fact, I said so yesterday in my testimony -- that the only resistance in the Sanski Most municipality was offered in Vrhpolje, that a group of people refused to surrender their weapons and they defended their own homes and their own village. According to my estimate, there were about 300 of them. That's my estimate, again. The number may vary, but the figure of 800 is out of the question. At that time I'm not even sure whether there was a total of 800 inhabitants there. I'm not sure. I don't know, as I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. All right. Can we now move, please, to document -- Prosecution's Exhibit 682, which is behind divider 3. It's a document dated the 17th of June, so it's the day that you were transferred to Manjaca -- talking about the situation with the prisons. And effectively, it -- I think you probably agree with its comments, forgetting about the reasons for it. But the -- "A large number of prisoners, mostly of Muslim nationality has appeared in the -- the SJB due to combat disarming operations, et cetera. This brings with it a series of problems such as accommodation of prisoners, their food, healthcare, visits by family members, which the SJB has neither the training nor the equipment to handle. That is why we are asking you help us and intervene with the authorities of the Autonomous Region of Krajina and the municipality so that the status of the prisoners is determined." Just one very simple question. I think you said your wife -- your family had already left. Were other prisoners in your cell receiving visits from family members?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: While I was there in the cell, no family members were able to get in there. However, on one occasion -- and I learnt that from the police -- my mother came to the police station to the duty officer and she handed over to them some cartons of juice. And then they gave these cartons to me. I think that there were some other cases like that involving some other prisoners. Later on this stopped. And then I heard that my mother had been expelled and had to go to Kladusa.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. I think we can just note the next document, 683, because that was in direction or order to Colonel Anicic from the Crisis Staff saying that some of the detainees in the sports hall should go after screening. Can we go to document, please, 688, which we will find behind -- P688, behind divider -- at 9.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And again, Your Honour, this is just a note, in fact, because it's again -- it's one of the decisions of the Crisis Staff that appeared in Sanski Most relating to the dismissals.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: 690, at divider 11, please. This is a Crisis Staff Sanski Most decision of the 22nd of June. And it explains: "The realisation of the conclusions of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina" --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The 23rd.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Yes. You're quite right. It's the 23rd of June and talks about a session of the 22nd. I just want to ask you this: At item F, it says: "Form camp in -- in [Realtime transcript read in error "Sanica"] Sitnica for the territory of the 2nd Krajina Corps of the army of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina." Where was -- was that in the area of Sanski Most?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Let me find it.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's 2(F). It's on the first page, I think. Yes, on the first page. I just want to know whether Sitnica.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sitnica.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: It's Sitnica, not Sanica. It's in the immediate vicinity of Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Oh?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: On the road between Cadjavica as you go from Mrkonjic Grad towards Kljuc in the direction of Banja Luka. That's where Sitnica is. That's in the municipality of Banja Luka.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. And just to note as item I: "The Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region of Krajina was criticised for reaching decisions that were important for the entire territory." Okay. Could we move, please, to document 694, at -- behind divider 15. This is a decision apparently undated, and it refers to a decision of the Crisis Staff of the Autonomous Region held on the 29th of June. "The Sanski Most Crisis Staff approved the decision on the confiscation of privately owned movable and immovable property in the areas from where armed operations were carried out and their transformation into state-owned property, Article 3, the Sanski Most municipality will administer and dispose of the property." Just very quickly and briefly, Judge. How -- what did that decision practically mean? What happened to property, movable and immovable?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This decision meant that the citizens of the Sanski Most municipality of Muslim and Croat ethnicity leaving Sanski Most -- or rather, those who were expelled had first to sign a statement indicating that they left all their property to the Autonomous Region of Krajina. So all their property remained in Sanski Most, and it was -- it was proclaimed that now it became the state-owned property or the property of the municipality of Sanski Most and of the Autonomous Region of Krajina. And that's in fact what happened. All the inhabitants who left Sanski Most had to leave their property behind, and it was taken away and in effect stolen, both movable and immovable property. There is a whole number of documents indicating that they did in fact dispose of our property as they saw fit.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And we're going to look at a couple more in there. If we look at the next document, we can see at P695 that "The municipal civilian protection staff will gather all movable goods and ensure adequate storage and security." And at the next document -- I'm sorry to move so quickly through. P696. But it's all, as you say, connected to the same theme. There's a decision, the 2nd of July, where Article 1 says that "Voluntary departure from Sanski Most municipality shall be allowed to families and persons who give a statement to the authorised municipal administration organ that they are permanently leaving the municipality and that they are leaving their real property to the Sanski Most municipality."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Yes, Ms. Korner, may I --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I with your indulgence interrupt you for a minute and seek the following clarification. Exhibit P694, which is unsigned, undated, and in the first line refers to an unnumbered article --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Purports to be a decision reached or taken on the 29th of June, 1992. And the -- of this alleged decision is confiscation with whatever is entailed legally under that term. The document you are referring the witness to now, 696, presents a completely different concept, and that is an imposition on whoever is leaving the municipality to agree leave the real property to the Sanski Most municipality.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Mm-hm.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can -- which is -- let's say that this second document is more in line with what the witness has been stating in his testimony. Is he in a position to confirm in an unequivocal manner that in fact the decision indicated in Exhibit P694 was actually taken? Because document -- this document could also be a draft decision --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Prepared in advance for a meeting which never materialised in a decision. Was a decision actually taken that you know of and that you can assure this Trial Chamber of - taken - on the 29th of June 1992 by the Sanski Most Municipal Crisis Staff to approve a routine confiscation process?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think that the Crisis Staff did take such a decision. It follows from the original decisions. Furthermore, this decision itself on the criteria for the possibility of departure from the municipality of Sanski Most, it's an operational decision. It merely elaborates another decision taken by the Crisis Staff. In effect, the Crisis Staff is the War Staff in this period when this decision was taken. It has the highest function in the municipality of Sanski Most.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But judge -- judge, we're talking of two completely different notions and two completely different scenarios. The scenario that you had been testifying on is you as a citizen -- a Muslim citizen of Sanski Most or a Croat citizen of Sanski Most municipality wanting to leave the municipality and one of the conditions imposed, according to you, is, "Okay, sir, you may leave. We'll even help you leave the municipality of Sanski Most, but you have to sign releasing all your landed property, immovable property, real property, call it whatever you like, to the municipality." That's one thing. This is something completely different in this alleged decision -- alleged decision of 29 June. This is referring to property found in areas in the Sanski Most municipality which had been the subject of armed conflict, armed intervention. And we're talking of confiscation now. We're not talking of a citizen of Sanski Most wanting to leave and he's faced with this dilemma that leaving means surrendering your property. This is irrespective of whether you're there or not, you are having your property confiscated because it happens to be where it is, namely an area where there has been armed intervention. If you know for sure that this was -- this decision was taken, then say so. If you have doubts or you don't know, then tell us. But it's important, because this is a document which is unsigned, unnumbered, undated. And the Prosecution has a duty to bring forward the best evidence that is available.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] First of all, I would like to say that this was not done by the citizens on a voluntary basis because all the areas that they attacked and all the areas where people were forced to go, nobody asked you whether you wanted to leave your property behind or not. The inhabitants were simply expelled from these areas. And that covers the most part of the territory of the Sanski Most municipality. And then later on at the sessions of various organs, including the executive board of the municipality, they used this milder terminology, "voluntary," the term "voluntary." There wasn't anything voluntary about it. This is an exaggeration, because I know for sure -- because I saw the documents pertaining to the sessions of the executive board and of the Crisis Staff and the discussions that they had, the interventions of individuals, what they were saying.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. You're not -- are you in a position to tell us whether this decision was actually taken or not, formally taken, by the Crisis Staff, the one shown on P694?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This decision was taken at the Crisis Staff.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But I think I'd better --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Do you understand there's nothing to indicate on the document that this is a decision that was actually passed. How are you able to say that this decision was actually made by the Crisis Staff?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already said, the inhabitants from these areas didn't sign anything.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. All right. But -- yes.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They had to leave everything behind.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. No. I think we really -- just pause for a moment, please. I understand what you're saying, but the point that the learned trial Judge is making that there's a difference between "confiscation", which simply means collection of movable cars, cows, whatever it is, and having to sign your -- away your property in order to leave. There are two different decisions. Are you saying that from what you know happened, that people who were in this war area were -- where armed operations carried out -- had their property taken. Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One could be confiscation or expropriation --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- At different levels or at different ends of the spectrum. The other one could become a de facto expropriation. But -- but let's stick to what is essential. I mean, Judge, like me and like every other judge, sometimes you draft a judgement which you leave on your desk and which you're supposed to give to hand down tomorrow, then you have second thoughts and you tear it up. If I happen -- because you change your mind or you want to expand on it. If I happen to take that draft judgement from your desk, it's unsigned, undated, how am I going to prove that it was actually handed down? This is the question. We have a document here which is unsigned and undated, refers to a decision supposedly taken on the 29th of June, 1992, but it's the first document of the kind which I am seeing which is completely unsigned and undated to the extent that it calls for some obvious questions or queries.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I -- Your Honour, I mean, I note the time. I think in fact we can deal with the reality of what happened from people who know what happened.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All we're asking you at this moment, Judge, is are you aware of any other document that supports the fact that on the -- at the end of June, the Crisis Staff issued a decision ordering confiscation?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can answer that question and say that yes, I was able to find out that this decision was implemented. And how did I do that? Well, for example, all the private vehicles or all technical equipment was confiscated and the documents were appropriated. There are documents in Sanski Most which I obtained. There are regulation plans for this municipal service, according to which Mahala should be transformed into --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Yes. Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I just want to make sure since we've talked about this so much that Your Honours understand that we strongly objected to this at the very beginning of the case because it was unsigned. It also comes from --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: From Bihac as well.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: From the AID office in Bihac, which I think is a very suspicious source of documents to start with. I think there's at least the possibility that it is just a pure forgery. There's no decision, as I understand it -- I've not seen one -- of the ARK Crisis Staff of 29 June 1992 regarding confiscation. It's very likely a complete forgery.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, you and Madam Fauveau together with your clients can put your minds to rest that no one will be condemned by this Trial Chamber on the basis of such a document.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: All right. And Mr. Ackerman's thoughts, opinions, suggestions are not in my submission admissible. He can think what he likes. We're talking about evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That -- with regard to Bihac and the AID, forget it. I'm not going to comment on that. That's obviously Mr. Ackerman's -- and he's entitled to that opinion.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. But he's not entitled to express it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But Ms. Korner is entitled to express her opinions about the evidence but I'm not entitled to express my opinion? Is that her position? She can stand her all day and say this shows Your Honour that such and such occurred. This Your Honour is an official document she's expressing her opinions all day every day and when I do it once she says I'm wrong I'm not allowed to do it. Stop her from doing it and then I'll stop doing it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Okay. Mr. Ackerman. Sit down and let's continue.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Let's leave that document shall we and move on in the remaining ten minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay document 6 -- P696, which we've looked at, does bear a stamp and a signature. And can we move then, please, to the next document, 697.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm sorry. Which divider is that?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's after divider 18. There is a report from the Sanski Most SJB to the CSB describing the -- the operations and the persons who have been processed. 332 after processing completed, 82 released, allowed to go home. 250 -- I'm not sure. Oh, and -- yes. If one looks at the original, it looks like 250 -- 850 -- if one looks at the original, you can see "850" has been inserted -- were sent to ha camp in Manjaca. If one looks at the original on it, there's 250, and then 850 sent to Manjaca.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's what it says.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right. Persons who fled from the place where combat operations were being conducted, about 500 of them who are able-bodied were being treated as civilian prisoners have been accommodated in the sports hall. Actually I don't think I need -- I'm sorry. I don't think I need asking you about that. Can we move on, please, to 699, which is behind divider 20. And that's, I think, merely to note that this was a document that you personally handed, I think, to the Office of the Prosecutor. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And dealing with the weapons on the disarmament. The next document you've already looked at.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I think that's already been dealt with. That's the informator. And he looked at it when he was dealing with propaganda.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Then document, please, 7 -- P701, a decision -- behind divider number 23. Sorry. A -- the War Staff ordering the SJB to take all measures and actions in conjunction with the municipal civilian protection staff to confiscate all looted property and take all measures prescribed. Article 2: "Ordered to take all necessary steps according to the available data to initiate a procedure against persons of Serbian nationality for whom there are reasonable grounds for suspicion that they are illegally selling weapons to persons of Muslim nationality." I'm sorry. I don't think there's very much I can ask you about that. P703. Now, this is a document again that I think you personally -- I'm sorry, behind divider 25 -- that you personally handed to the Office of the Prosecutor. And it's the executive committee of the Sanski Most --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: -- Assembly. It looks as though you found a whole set of these. And there's reference there to the Autonomous Region of Krajina adopting a decision banning the purchase of all essential and inessential -- and then it look like "movable and immovable property as of the 14th of April, 1992." It's not clear as to what that applies. Could you move, please, then to document 706, which is behind divider 28. And again, this is a document that you personally handed, it would appear, to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And is a report on the work of the Sanski Most station between January and June.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I don't think we need to go into details about that report. So if we could move, please, to 708, behind divider 30, merely to note that you personally handed this document over. Again, it's an executive committee minutes.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next document, P709.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: What divider is that, please?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: The next divider. 31, please. Which again is another document dealing with the movement of the population. It's a conclusion of the executive committee again of the municipal assembly, which in the third paragraph talks about 18 -- I'm sorry. I'm just checking the original on this. I'm getting slightly concerned about numbers. But -- it says? 18.000 Muslims and Croats in the Sanski Most area. In order to avoid danger to the Serbian population, it is necessary to organise their voluntary resettlement." And then --

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sorry. I would just like to add something.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Voluntarily. You see, this is the fabrication. It's a lie. Voluntarily means to expel, to -- to remove by force. That's what it means.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: And that -- in item 5: "The court start working is a matter of urgency and the government of the Autonomous Region of Krajina be urgently requested to approve the establishment of prisons." The next document, please, which is document -- I'd like you to look at -- 710. And that's purely to note that you handed this document -- behind divider 32.

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's a document that I provided to the Prosecution. It's a note from the 9th session of the executive committee of the Sanski Most Municipal Assembly.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. And I don't think we need to look at that. Document 713, behind divider 35. Again, I think that's a document that you personally handed to the Office of the Prosecutor's representative. Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: ADIL DRAGANOVIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Now, it's the 5th of August, 1992, a report to the Banja Luka CSB and states that "Paramilitary groups have escaped the control of the army command, have become increasingly active in Sanski Most, carrying out private operations, planting bombs, burning houses, murdering people, plundering property, and other crimes against the Muslim and Croatian population, all for their personal gain and to put pressure on this population to leave. 45 bombs planted in the last two months in Muslim's homes and cafes, two mosques destroyed, five buildings burnt, four murders. As regards plunder of movable property, it's almost impossible to keep any kind of record because the victims do not dare to report the perpetrators." And then it deals with the groups in question and says: "We have so far registered four such group, one of them being the so-called SOS a court reporter paramilitary formation about 30 men strong that was formerly placed under the command of a war unit here as a sabotage platoon. However, the unit does not have full control of the formation."

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think that's probably, I'm afraid, as far as we can take it today.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] Thank you, Ms. Korner. Shall I take it that you may have a few more questions?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Yes. I've got about another ten documents and that's it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And that means --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Sorry, interpreters. I take it that Ms. Korner has a few more questions relating to ten documents which basically means that either of you, depending on how you have agreed to -- amongst yourself who is going first will start the cross-examination tomorrow morning.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, our agreement is that Madam Fauveau will go first.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: She has estimated she will take a full session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No. I'm not interested in that for time being, because obviously the Prosecution now is in a position to know for sure that the witness will need to be here again on Tuesday. So the question of how long Madam Fauveau or you are going to take does no longer arise -- at least not entirely. So --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'm not sure -- has Your Honour -- have we given Your Honours the statement for the next witness?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I don't --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: We'll arrange to do that tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, please. Yes, please. The pleasure is yet to come.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Can we be told who it is?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: If you follow the list, you'll see who he is. I'm not mentioning his name because --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I can tell you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: We've kind of departed from the list a little bit in terms of he left out some people and he's out of order from the list and -- I just want to know where we're going.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. It's 7.193.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Well, I -- unfortunately I haven't got my list here.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: No protective measure, I but I'm not going to mention the name.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: No. That's not right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Pardon?

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Sorry, Your Honour. That isn't right. Not according to our list. That's why I was wondering.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is the last list that I have, dated 22nd of April of this year.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Okay. Your Honour I'll do a double-check and let Your Honours know tomorrow -- you'll get the statement anyhow. But I have a feeling that something went wrong there as well, because I've just been shown a note that shows it's a different witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think you ought to check that and --

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: I will.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: -- Inform everyone tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: Your Honour, can I say straight away that I think there will be -- have to be some changes for reasons which have suddenly arisen in any event. So I think we better prepare a new list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The only thing that I have here in front of me in this list is no amendments except a note that I have made that Witness 7.52, Mr. McLeod will testify on the 21st of June.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
utterances.text: That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That's the only thing that I first have.

utterances.speaker: MS. KORNER
